prompt.context: Our client is the new state superintendent of public schools, and is worried about teacher attrition in K-12 public schools in the state. Overall, the state attrition rate for teachers in 2018-2019 was 10%. There were 71,000 teachers employed during this time. The superintendent wants to understand how to improve teacher retention.
prompt.question: How should the superintendent improve teacher retention in K-12 public schools in the state?

clarifying_info.q: What does teacher attrition mean in this context?
clarifying_info.a: Teacher attrition is the rate at which teachers exit the teaching profession in this state (i.e. they could move to a different state and continue teaching).

clarifying_info.q: Are we focused on all schools or just public schools?
clarifying_info.a: We are only focused on teacher attrition in the K-12 public schools in the state.

clarifying_info.q: How many school districts and schools are there?
clarifying_info.a: The state has 115 public school districts and 2,500+ traditional public schools.

clarifying_info.q: How does state student performance compare to national benchmarks?
clarifying_info.a: The average test scores across the state are not significantly different from that of public school students in the nation.

clarifying_info.q: What is the nationwide teacher attrition rate?
clarifying_info.a: Nationwide teacher attrition is at 8% during the time of this case.
Yes, attrition includes teachers who retire.

clarifying_info.q: When do teachers receive full benefits and pension?
clarifying_info.a: Teachers receive their full benefits and pension after teaching for 30 years.

exhibits.title: Teacher Attrition by Category, 2018-2019
exhibits.shows: A table showing two categories of teachers — Experienced Licensed Teachers and Beginning Teachers — with columns for total number of teachers in the category, number leaving state public schools, and percent attrition in 2018-2019. The percent attrition column is blank and must be calculated.

exhibits.title: Attrition Rate by Years of Teaching Experience (March 2018 – March 2019, n=7,100)
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the percentage of teachers no longer employed in state public schools, plotted against years of teaching experience from 1 to 36. The y-axis runs from 0% to 50%.

data.notable_pattern: There is a visible spike in attrition rate around years 27–30.

exhibits.title: Reasons for Teacher Attrition
exhibits.shows: A table listing reasons for teacher attrition grouped into three categories: Personal Reasons, Initiated by School District, and Beyond Control of School District. Each reason shows the number of teachers and percent of total attrition.

framework: Who is leaving? — Segment attrition by experience level (beginning vs. experienced), subject area, school district, and teacher demographics to identify where attrition is highest.
Why are they leaving? — Understand root causes: personal reasons (family, relocation, career change, dissatisfaction), dismissal by school, and retirement (full vs. reduced benefits).

What policies currently exist? — Assess current new-teacher support programs and retention programs at the state, district, and school level; evaluate whether a system exists for tracking at-risk teachers before end of year.

questions.prompt: Calculate the attrition rate for Experienced Licensed Teachers and Beginning Teachers using Exhibit 1a. What do you notice?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates compute both rates accurately, immediately note that beginning teacher attrition (12%) is higher than experienced teacher attrition (~9%), and recognize that both sit relative to the overall 10% state rate and the 8% national benchmark. They should flag that beginning teachers have ~33% higher attrition than experienced teachers, suggesting early-career retention is the key pressure point.

math.setup: Attrition rate = Number leaving / Total teachers in category
steps: Beginning teacher attrition (12%) is ~33% higher than experienced teacher attrition (9%).
math.answer: Beginning teachers: ~12%; Experienced teachers: ~9%. Beginning teachers leave at a rate roughly one-third higher than experienced teachers.

questions.prompt: What does Exhibit 1b reveal about attrition by years of experience?
questions.guidance: Candidates should note the general pattern — higher attrition in early years (years 1–5), declining through mid-career, then a sharp spike around years 27–30. The key insight is to probe whether the late-career spike reflects teachers hitting full retirement eligibility (age 65/5 years, age 60/25 years, or 30 years at any age) or leaving early with reduced benefits before completing 30 years. This connects back to the pension structure shared in the case background.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, what are the most significant addressable drivers of attrition, and which categories are most actionable for the state?
questions.guidance: Candidates should rank reasons by size: (1) Retired with full benefits 20% — largely structural/unavoidable; (2) Resigned due to career change 13% — potentially addressable; (3) Retired with reduced benefits 12% — partially addressable (incentives to stay longer); (4) Resigned due to family relocation 10% — limited state control; (5) Resigned to teach in another state 10% — addressable through compensation or working conditions. The most actionable buckets for the state are career change, reduced-benefit early retirement, and teaching in another state, as these have identifiable levers. Personal/family reasons and full retirement are harder to influence.

brainstorming.prompt: What could the state do to address teacher attrition?

categories.name: Beginning Teacher Retention
ideas: Mentorship matching programs pairing beginning teachers with experienced veterans
Pulse surveys to beginning teachers at district/state level to understand ongoing needs
Dedicated resources and support during high-stress periods (start of year, testing periods)
Social media or digital community profiling to help beginning teachers feel connected to the broader statewide teaching community

categories.name: Experienced Teacher Retention (20+ years)
ideas: Anonymous pulse surveys to highly experienced teachers to understand what keeps them in the classroom and why they might consider leaving
Statewide opportunities to visit excellent classrooms and continue professional learning
Develop professional learning communities connecting excellent and novice teachers
Address teacher pay and education funding broadly

categories.name: Compensation and Benefits
ideas: Increase base pay to be competitive with other states and reduce resigned-to-teach-in-another-state attrition
Improve early-retirement incentive structure to reduce reduced-benefit departures
Offer loan forgiveness or housing assistance targeted at beginning teachers in high-need districts

categories.name: Career Development
ideas: Create alternative career pathways within education (coaching, curriculum design, administration) so teachers considering a career change stay within the system
Develop leadership pipelines for mid-career teachers

recommendation: The state should prioritize improving retention of beginning teachers, who leave at a ~33% higher rate than experienced teachers, by leveraging technology to develop robust peer networks between beginning and experienced teachers to keep them connected to the teaching community.

For near-term wins, the state should also target the two most actionable personal-reason drivers — career change (13%) and early retirement with reduced benefits (12%) — through targeted incentives and career-development pathways.
risks: Political capital needed to build and sustain a major statewide technology system
System may take a long time to design, pilot, and scale effectively
Teachers may experience additional network or survey obligations as burdensome if accessible only outside school hours
Compensation-based solutions require budget appropriations that may face legislative resistance
next_steps: Conduct an anonymous survey to identify which teachers are considering leaving and their primary reasons
Identify a target cohort of beginning and experienced teachers to serve as an initial focus group for a peer-network pilot
Analyze whether compensation and benefit adjustments in competing states are driving the 10% of teachers resigning to teach in another state
